title: Matrix Chain Multiplication
directAnswer: Given matrix dimensions p[0..n] (matrix i is p[i-1] × p[i]), find the parenthesization that minimizes scalar multiplications. The recurrence splits the chain i..j at every k: dp[i][j] = min over k in i..j-1 of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i-1]·p[k]·p[j]. dp[i][i] = 0. Naive recursion is exponential; memoize on (i, j) or fill the table by increasing chain length. O(n³) time, O(n²) space.

remember.pattern: Interval DP — split a chain at every cut point
remember.formula:
dp[i][i] = 0
for length L in 2..n:
    for i in 1..n-L+1:
        j = i + L - 1
        dp[i][j] = min over k in i..j-1 of
                   dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i-1]*p[k]*p[j]
return dp[1][n]
rules: You're choosing where to put the **last** multiplication (the outermost split `k`), not the first — the two halves `i..k` and `k+1..j` are solved independently.
The merge cost of joining the two halves is `p[i-1] · p[k] · p[j]`: the left result is `p[i-1] × p[k]`, the right is `p[k] × p[j]`, multiplying them costs that product.
It's an **interval DP**: state is a contiguous range `[i, j]`, and you must fill by **increasing length** so both sub-intervals are ready before the merge.
`dp[i][i] = 0` — a single matrix needs no multiplication. The diagonal is the base case.
Dimensions array has `n+1` entries for `n` matrices; matrix `i` is `p[i-1] × p[i]`. Off-by-one here is the classic trap.
whenToUse: Optimize over all ways to parenthesize / bracket a sequence
Cost of combining two adjacent groups depends on a boundary value between them
State is a contiguous interval [i, j] and the answer combines two sub-intervals
Splitting at a middle point k decouples the problem into independent left/right halves
antiSignals: Each element decided independently (take/skip) → knapsack-style linear DP, not interval
Cost of merging doesn't depend on a shared boundary → probably a simpler 1-D DP
You need the actual parenthesization, not just the cost → store a split table alongside dp
n is large (thousands) → O(n³) may be too slow; look for special structure (Hu–Shing for matrices)
remember.takeaway: Matrix Chain is the gateway interval DP. The move that unlocks it: don't pick the first multiplication, pick the LAST one — the outermost split k cleanly separates [i..k] and [k+1..j]. Fill by increasing interval length so sub-intervals are ready. The same 'split at every k, fill by length' template solves Burst Balloons, Palindrome Partitioning II, and Boolean Parenthesization.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize an interval-DP structure, set the state as a range [i, j], split on the last (outermost) operation, and order the table fill by increasing length so dependencies are ready.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Mangling the merge-cost index (using the wrong p[] triple), or filling the table in plain i,j order so dp[i][k] / dp[k+1][j] aren't computed yet.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Say 'I'll split on the last multiplication, k, which makes the two sides independent intervals'. Derive the p[i-1]·p[k]·p[j] cost from the shapes, then fill by chain length and mention this is the canonical interval-DP template.

problemStatement:
You are given an array `p` of length `n + 1` describing the dimensions of `n` matrices: matrix `i` (for `i` from `1` to `n`) has dimensions `p[i-1] × p[i]`, so adjacent matrices are conformable for multiplication.

Matrix multiplication is associative, so the *result* is the same for any parenthesization, but the ***number of scalar multiplications*** differs. Multiplying an `a × b` matrix by a `b × c` matrix costs `a · b · c` scalar multiplications.

Return the ***minimum*** number of scalar multiplications needed to compute the product of the whole chain.
understanding: Find the cheapest way to bracket a chain of matrix multiplications. The product matrix is fixed by associativity; only the cost varies with the order of multiplications. The state is a contiguous interval of matrices [i, j], and the answer for an interval is built by choosing the outermost split and adding the cost of merging the two resulting matrices.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How are the matrix dimensions encoded?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: As a single array p of length n+1. Matrix i is p[i-1] × p[i]. So p = [10, 20, 30] means two matrices: 10×20 and 20×30.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need to output the parenthesization or just the cost?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the minimum scalar-multiplication count here. (Reconstructing the bracketing means storing the best split k for each interval in a second table.)

clarifyingQuestions.question: What does it cost to multiply two matrices?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: An a×b matrix times a b×c matrix costs a·b·c scalar multiplications and yields an a×c matrix. That product formula drives the whole DP.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What's the answer for a single matrix?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 0 — there's nothing to multiply. That's the diagonal base case dp[i][i] = 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the matrices guaranteed conformable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — consecutive dimensions match by construction (matrix i is p[i-1]×p[i], matrix i+1 is p[i]×p[i+1]), so any adjacent pair can be multiplied.

examples.explanation: Parenthesize as (A1·A2)·A3: A1·A2 costs 10·20·30 = 6000 → 10×30; then ·A3 costs 10·30·40 = 12000. Total 18000. The other order A1·(A2·A3) costs 24000 + 8000 = 32000.
Best bracketing is (A1·(A2·A3))·A4. The naive left-to-right order costs far more; the split table finds 26000.
Optimal split yields 124 scalar multiplications; trying all parenthesizations by hand is exponential, the DP finds it directly.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. Matrix Chain lands on the interval-DP-by-length branch.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recursion Over the Outermost Split
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to establish the split-on-k recurrence and the merge-cost formula, then flag the exponential branching.
hints: Don't think about which multiplication happens first — think about which happens LAST. The last multiply combines a left group A_i..A_k with a right group A_{k+1}..A_j.
For a fixed last split at k, the cost is (best way to multiply the left group) + (best way to multiply the right group) + the cost of combining the two resulting matrices.
The left result is p[i-1] × p[k], the right is p[k] × p[j]; combining them costs p[i-1]·p[k]·p[j]. Take the min over all k in i..j-1. Base: solve(i, i) = 0.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each interval branches into up to (j - i) splits, and the splits overlap heavily; the number of distinct parenthesizations is the Catalan number, which grows like 4ⁿ/n^1.5 — exponential. Recursion depth is O(n).
approaches.explanation:
Define `solve(i, j)` as the minimum cost to multiply matrices `i..j`. The key decision is the *outermost* (last) multiplication: pick a split point `k` between `i` and `j-1`, which means you first compute the product of `A_i..A_k` (a matrix of shape `p[i-1] × p[k]`), then the product of `A_{k+1}..A_j` (shape `p[k] × p[j]`), and finally multiply those two results together at cost `p[i-1] · p[k] · p[j]`. The answer for `(i, j)` is the minimum of that over all valid `k`. The base case is `solve(i, i) = 0` — one matrix needs no work.

**The mental shift: choose the LAST multiplication, not the first.** This is the move that makes interval DP click. If you tried to pick the first multiplication, the two halves wouldn't be independent — the result of one feeds the next in a tangled way. But fixing the *outermost* split `k` cleanly partitions the chain into two contiguous sub-chains `[i, k]` and `[k+1, j]` that can be solved completely independently, then merged with one well-defined cost.

**Where the merge cost comes from.** After fully multiplying the left group you have a single matrix of dimensions `p[i-1] × p[k]` (its row count is the first matrix's rows, its column count is the `k`-th matrix's columns). The right group collapses to `p[k] × p[j]`. Multiplying an `(p[i-1] × p[k])` by a `(p[k] × p[j])` matrix costs `p[i-1] · p[k] · p[j]` scalar multiplications — that's the single term you add at this level.

**Why min.** Different `k` values are alternative bracketings of the same product; we want the cheapest, so we combine with `min`.

**Why we don't ship this.** The same interval `(i, j)` is re-solved inside many different outer splits — massive overlap. Cache `solve(i, j)` and the exponential collapses to O(n³).
approaches.insight: Two index variables `(i, j)` describe the state — a contiguous interval — and the naive tree recomputes the same interval through different outer splits. A 2-D interval state plus exponential overlap is the textbook signal for an O(n³) interval DP.

dryRun.intro: solve(i, j) = min over k of solve(i,k) + solve(k+1,j) + p[i-1]·p[k]·p[j]. Base solve(i,i)=0.

java.explanation: n matrices are described by n+1 dimensions; matrix i is p[i-1]×p[i].
Base case: a single matrix needs zero multiplications — the diagonal of the table.

java.line: for (int k = i; k < j; k++) {
java.explanation: Try every outermost split: left group i..k, right group k+1..j.

java.line: int cost = solve(p, i, k) + solve(p, k + 1, j) + p[i - 1] * p[k] * p[j];
java.explanation: Left cost + right cost + merge cost (left is p[i-1]×p[k], right is p[k]×p[j]).

python.explanation: k is the last multiplication's split point; both sides become independent intervals.

python.line: cost = solve(i, k) + solve(k + 1, j) + p[i - 1] * p[k] * p[j]
python.explanation: The merge term p[i-1]·p[k]·p[j] is the cost of multiplying the two assembled matrices.

edgeCases.behavior: solve(1, 1) returns 0 immediately — nothing to multiply.

pitfalls: Splitting on the first multiplication instead of the last — the halves stop being independent.
Getting the merge-cost triple wrong — it must be p[i-1]·p[k]·p[j], the rows/shared/cols of the two assembled matrices.
Skipping this approach — the split-on-k recurrence is exactly what the interviewer wants verbalized.

approaches.name: Top-Down Memoization on (i, j)
approaches.whenToMention: The fix once you name the overlap — 'cache the answer for each interval (i, j)'.
hints: solve(i, j) returns the same value every call. Where can you store it so each interval is computed once?
Use a 2-D memo of size (n+1) × (n+1) indexed by interval endpoints. Check on entry, fill before returning.
memo[i][j] = min over k of solve(i,k) + solve(k+1,j) + p[i-1]·p[k]·p[j]; use -1 (or 0 only on the diagonal) to mark 'uncomputed'.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are O(n²) distinct intervals (i, j). Each does O(n) work scanning split points → O(n³) total. The memo is O(n²); recursion depth is O(n) on top.
approaches.explanation:
Keep the split-on-`k` recurrence but cache `solve(i, j)` in a 2-D table so every interval is solved exactly once. The memo starts 'uncomputed'; on entry we return the cached value and store the result before returning.

**The mental shift: the cost of an interval depends only on its endpoints.** No matter which outer splits led you to consider matrices `i..j`, the cheapest way to multiply that contiguous block is a fixed number. So caching by `(i, j)` collapses all the duplicate subtrees. There are `O(n²)` intervals, and each costs `O(n)` to resolve (scan the splits), giving the `O(n³)` bound directly.

**Why the state is two indices, not one.** Unlike Coin Change (one number), an interval needs *both* a left and a right boundary — different ranges of the same length have different costs because the dimensions inside them differ. That's why the memo is 2-D.

**Choosing the sentinel.** Initialize the memo to -1 for 'uncomputed' (0 is a valid cost only on the diagonal, so guarding `i == j` separately or using -1 keeps things unambiguous).

**A language note.** Top-down recursion here nests up to `O(n)` deep. In Java that's fine for `n ≤ 100`. In Python the default recursion limit is about 1000 and the per-call overhead is higher — for large chains the bottom-up table (next approach) is the cleaner default because it visits intervals in a guaranteed-ready order without any stack.
approaches.insight: Same mechanical DP upgrade: a correct recurrence plus a cache keyed on the true state, here the interval `(i, j)`. The intellectual work was seeing that the outermost split makes the two halves independent intervals — once that clicks, the 2-D memo and its O(n³) cost follow mechanically.

dryRun.intro: memo[i][j] caches the min cost for interval i..j. Filled lazily; smaller intervals resolve first.

java.explanation: -1 marks 'uncomputed'; real costs are non-negative, and the i==j base returns 0 before any lookup.
Cache hit — return the stored min cost for this interval in O(1).

java.line: int cost = solve(p, i, k, memo) + solve(p, k + 1, j, memo) + p[i - 1] * p[k] * p[j];
java.explanation: Sub-interval costs from the cache plus the merge term for this split.
Store the resolved min before returning so this interval is never recomputed.

python.explanation: Caches solve by its (i, j) arguments — a clean 2-D top-down memo.

python.line: cost = solve(i, k) + solve(k + 1, j) + p[i - 1] * p[k] * p[j]
python.explanation: Independent halves plus merge cost. Note: deep recursion can approach Python's ~1000 limit; tabulation avoids the stack.

edgeCases.behavior: Only k = 1 exists; memo[1][2] = p[0]·p[1]·p[2], one multiplication.
solve(1, 1) returns 0 without touching the memo.

pitfalls: Choosing a sentinel that a real cost could equal — costs are ≥ 0, so use -1, and let the i==j base return 0.
Sizing the memo as n×n instead of (n+1)×(n+1) — matrices are 1-indexed here.
Deep recursion in Python (depth ~n) plus overhead makes tabulation preferable for large chains.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up — Interval DP by Increasing Length (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'fill dp[i][j] by chain length so both sub-intervals are ready before the merge'.
hints: The cost of interval [i, j] needs the costs of strictly shorter intervals [i, k] and [k+1, j]. So solve all length-1 intervals, then length-2, ... up to length-n.
dp[i][i] = 0. For length L from 2 to n, set i from 1, j = i + L - 1, and try every split k in i..j-1.
dp[i][j] = min over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i-1]·p[k]·p[j]. The answer is dp[1][n].
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are O(n²) intervals; each scans up to O(n) split points → O(n³) time. The dp table is (n+1)² → O(n²) space, and there's no recursion stack.
approaches.explanation:
Build the table by increasing interval length so every sub-interval is finalized before it's needed. Set the diagonal `dp[i][i] = 0`. Then for each length `L` from `2` to `n`, walk the left endpoint `i`, compute the right endpoint `j = i + L - 1`, and try every outermost split `k` in `i..j-1`, relaxing `dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i-1]·p[k]·p[j])`. The answer is `dp[1][n]`.

**The mental shift: length is the dependency order.** Interval `[i, j]` of length `L` depends only on intervals `[i, k]` and `[k+1, j]`, both strictly shorter than `L`. So if we fill by increasing length, both pieces are always already computed when we reach the merge — no recursion needed, just three nested loops (length, left endpoint, split point). This length-ordered fill is *the* defining move of interval DP; plain row-major `i, j` iteration would read cells that aren't ready yet.

**Re-deriving the merge cost in table terms.** When we combine `[i, k]` (a matrix of shape `p[i-1] × p[k]`) with `[k+1, j]` (shape `p[k] × p[j]`), the multiplication costs `p[i-1] · p[k] · p[j]` and produces the `p[i-1] × p[j]` matrix that interval `[i, j]` represents. Add that to the two cached sub-costs.

**Why the diagonal is the base.** A length-1 interval is a single matrix — zero multiplications. Every larger interval's cost is anchored on these zeros, the same way `dp[0]` anchors a linear DP.

**Why min over all k.** Each split is a different bracketing of the same product; we keep the cheapest.
approaches.insight: This is the canonical interval-DP template: state = contiguous range, decision = the outermost split k, fill order = increasing length. Swap the cost function and you've solved Burst Balloons (split on the LAST balloon to pop), Palindrome Partitioning II (split into palindromic pieces), and Boolean Parenthesization (split a boolean expression). Learn the skeleton once, reuse it everywhere.

diagrams.title: Upper-triangular dp table filled by length
diagrams.caption: dp[i][j] for p=[10,20,30,40]. Diagonal is 0; fill direction goes up-right by increasing length. Answer at dp[1][3].

edgeCases.behavior: Length loop never runs; dp[1][1] = 0 returned.
Only L=2, single split k=1: dp[1][2] = p[0]·p[1]·p[2].
Every merge costs d³ and any bracketing ties — DP returns (n-1)·d³.

pitfalls: Iterating i, j in plain order instead of by length — reads dp[i][k] / dp[k+1][j] before they're computed.
Forgetting to reset dp[i][j] to +∞ before the split loop — leaves a stale 0 that wins the min.
Off-by-one in the merge triple — it must be p[i-1]·p[k]·p[j], not p[i]·p[k]·p[j].

commonMistakes: Filling the table in plain (i, j) order instead of by increasing interval length, so sub-intervals aren't ready.
Using the wrong dimension triple for the merge cost (must be p[i-1]·p[k]·p[j]).
Splitting on the first multiplication rather than the last (outermost) one, breaking the independence of the halves.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong table fill order
commonMistakesDetailed.why: dp[i][j] reads dp[i][k] and dp[k+1][j], which are SHORTER intervals. Iterating i ascending and j ascending visits dp[i][j] before some shorter intervals are done, reading stale zeros. Fill by increasing length.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong merge-cost triple
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Combining [i,k] (shape p[i-1]×p[k]) with [k+1,j] (shape p[k]×p[j]) costs p[i-1]·p[k]·p[j]. Using p[i]·p[k]·p[j] silently computes a different, wrong cost.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int cost = dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j] + p[i] * p[k] * p[j];
commonMistakesDetailed.good: int cost = dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j] + p[i - 1] * p[k] * p[j];

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not resetting the interval cost before the split loop
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If dp[i][j] still holds its initialized 0, the min over splits never improves past 0 and the answer collapses to 0. Set it to +∞ first.

patternNote: Canonical interval DP. Recognize it whenever the state is a contiguous range [i, j] and the answer is built by choosing an outermost split point k that separates two independent sub-intervals, with a boundary-dependent merge cost. Fill by increasing length. Same template as Burst Balloons, Palindrome Partitioning II, and polygon triangulation.
